summary:
FMLink reports that the Copper Development Association (CDA) participated in the United Association's annual instructor training program at Washtenaw Community College in Ann Arbor, Michigan, delivering a 20-hour course on copper tube and copper alloy joining methods, plus problem identification and troubleshooting.

The United Association represents plumbers, pipefitters, refrigeration technicians, sprinkler fitters and related trades across more than 300 local unions in the US and Canada. Its instructor training program prepares educators who run apprenticeship and continuing education programs at those locals.

Course structure: 20 hours over five days, split into separate four-hour morning and afternoon sessions. Forty-three participants enrolled this year, 22 in the morning session and 21 in the afternoon. Emphasis was placed on soldering, brazing and other copper joining methods. CDA's training team worked alongside two active UA instructors to combine classroom education with shop-based instruction. Participants completed 10 copper assembly modules in teams of two and were evaluated on classroom and shop participation. The week concluded with a teaching exercise in which volunteers played instructor and apprentice roles during a copper soldering project.

The UA program has trained instructors since 1955 and offers certifications and associate degree programs with an equal mix of trade-specific and professional teaching courses. Instructor certification requires 200 hours of instruction over five years; training coordinators earn certification after an additional 120 hours. The program includes the annual Ann Arbor event plus regional and online courses.

CDA project manager Mike Belanger framed the value as a multiplier effect, saying training the trainers lets knowledge reach far beyond the room. CDA's involvement dates to 1955 through its predecessor, the Copper and Brass Research Association. Three CDA representatives participated this year: Marcus Elmer, Harold Moret and Mike Belanger.

The piece concerns skilled trades education and is unrelated to workplace technology themes such as visitor management, desk booking, hybrid policy or workplace analytics.
